summary: For 11–12 year olds, teach the water cycle as a SUN-DRIVEN, gravity-pulled loop in which the same water is conserved: evaporation (liquid→vapour), condensation (vapour cooling into visible liquid cloud droplets), precipitation, surface runoff and groundwater, plus transpiration (plants releasing vapour from leaves). The load-bearing ideas beyond a KS2 version are (a) the sun is the energy source driving evaporation while gravity pulls precipitation and runoff down, and (b) vegetation is genuinely part of the cycle, so deforestation and paving reduce transpiration and increase/accelerate runoff and flooding. The strongest proposal is a landscape model the learner can both follow one droplet around and perturb (sun intensity, land use); a labelled tappable diagram, a hands-on condensation investigation, assessment items, and an extension discussion each carry distinct teaching purposes and are preserved below.
misconceptions: Thinking the water cycle runs by itself without recognising the sun as the energy source driving evaporation.
Omitting transpiration, so plants are left out of the cycle.
Believing clouds are made of water vapour (invisible gas) rather than condensed liquid droplets.
Assuming human land use (deforestation, paving) has no effect on the water cycle, treating it as fixed.

activities.title: Follow-and-perturb the water cycle landscape
steps: Ride a single labelled water droplet around the full loop: lifted off a sunlit sea as vapour, gathered into a cooling cloud, dropped as rain/precipitation, running across land as surface runoff, and returning to the sea.

Adjust a sun-intensity control and observe evaporation speed up or slow; set the sun to zero and watch new evaporation stop and the cycle wind down (water already aloft still falls), so the sun is seen as the energy source.
Watch the model's ribbons, which stand for invisible transpiration vapour, rising from vegetation as a contribution to the air's moisture (real water vapour cannot be seen).

Swap a forested hillside for concrete/paving and observe two changes at once in the model: the ribbons representing transpiration vapour disappear, and rain soaks in much less and sheets off as runoff, raising the river below and making flooding more likely.
State in words what drives each stage and how clearing or paving land reroutes the water.
activities.insight: The water cycle is a driven system — the sun powers evaporation and gravity pulls precipitation and runoff — not a self-moving diagram; plants are part of the cycle via transpiration, and human land-use changes genuinely reroute water.

activities.title: Labelled cycle diagram with revealed drivers
steps: Label a water-cycle diagram including evaporation, condensation, precipitation, surface runoff and transpiration.
Tap or lift a flap on each stage to reveal what drives it — e.g. 'sun heats water, liquid becomes vapour' at evaporation; a tree for transpiration.
Toggle a human-impact layer and describe how land use alters the stages.
activities.insight: The canonical representation of the cycle, with each stage named and its driver explicit, so vocabulary and sequence are secure as a reference.

activities.title: Mini water cycle: predict–observe–explain investigation
steps: Put warm water in a clear bowl, cover tightly with cling film, and rest an ice cube on top.
Before observing, PREDICT what happens to the water level and whether the evaporated water is 'gone', and write WHY.
Watch droplets form under the chilled film and drip back; compare with your prediction.
Explain where the water went and how it returned, using the words evaporation, condensation, precipitation and conservation.

Note that this bowl is a model, not the real cycle: here the ice cube supplies the cooling and the warm water supplies the evaporation, standing in for the sun-driven atmosphere where the sun is the energy source and higher, colder air does the cooling.
activities.insight: Evaporation is a change of state, not destruction: liquid water becomes invisible vapour that is still present, then condenses on cooling and falls back — the same water is recycled. The bowl is a simplified stand-in for the real sun-driven cycle.

activities.title: Why does the city flood? — human-impact reasoning
steps: Discuss or write why a paved city tends to flood more than a forested hillside in the same rainstorm.
Reason about two mechanisms: less transpiration when trees are removed, and faster/greater surface runoff when ground is paved.
Apply the idea to a given scenario, e.g. 'If a town clears its woods and paves its soil, what changes in the local water cycle?'
activities.insight: Human land-use changes reroute water through the cycle by reducing transpiration and increasing runoff — the cycle is something land use can change, not a fixed diagram.

activities.title: Check and sequence the model
steps: Label and sequence the stages of the cycle in order.
Answer 'What drives evaporation?' (the sun's energy).
Match each stage to its process (e.g. condensation → vapour cools into droplets).
Reason about an item such as 'How does paving over soil change runoff?'
activities.insight: Checks whether the learner holds the full labelled cycle, names the sun as the driver, includes transpiration, and can reason about a human-impact case.

checkQuestion: Say: 'A puddle dries up on a sunny day and vanishes. Where has the water gone — is it gone for good? Then explain what makes water come back down as rain, and what part the sun and plants play.'
checkAnswer: The water is not gone — the sun's heat evaporated it into invisible water vapour in the air. It returns as rain when the vapour rises, cools and CONDENSES into cloud droplets that fall as precipitation. The sun drives evaporation and powers the whole cycle; plants add water vapour by transpiration. The same water is recycled — none is created or destroyed.
